title: The science of savoring
hookLine: savoring good moments extends their effect

cards: A song comes on in the car, the one from that summer. For about four seconds everything is good. Then the light turns green, somebody honks, and the mind is already back on the grocery list.
Good moments arrive all the time. Many of them leave before they've finished arriving. Two psychologists set out to study what people do when a good moment actually lands and stays a while.
They gave it an old word: savoring.

teach.h: NOTICE IT, AND STAY WITH IT.
teach.b: First, the idea. Fred Bryant and Joseph Veroff, in their book Savoring, describe it as noticing a good experience and deliberately staying with it, so it lasts longer and runs deeper.
Not creating good things; paying attention to the ones already here. Second, three directions in time.
Looking forward, when anticipation is part of the pleasure. Staying in the moment while it happens. And looking back, when remembering brings some of it home again.
One good weekend can be enjoyed three times. Third, the moves. Sharing the moment: telling a friend, or turning to the person next to you and saying, look at that.

teach.h: SHARE IT, SNAP IT, SHARPEN IT.
teach.b: Building a memory on purpose, like taking a mental photograph. Sharpening the senses, slowing down for the color, the sound, the warmth. Fourth, an old voice.
The book of Ecclesiastes keeps coming back to how everything passes.

And yet, right in the middle, it says, in the King James Bible: "Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart." Because things pass, the Preacher doesn't say skip the joy.
He says take it fully while it's here. One honest note: savoring isn't forced cheerfulness, and it isn't a fix for grief or depression. It's a skill for the good moments you already have.

how: People who practice savoring pause on good moments, share them with others and replay them later; some religious traditions build the same habit into blessings and thanks said over ordinary things.

games.q: what does “the science of savoring” mean?
o: planning new treats so your day has more good in it
forcing yourself to feel cheerful when things are hard
noticing a good moment and deliberately staying with it

games.q: the science of savoring: tap the pairs.

s: savoring only means enjoying the present moment
it runs three ways: looking forward, staying in the moment and looking back.
sharing a good moment with someone is one of the ways people savor
telling a friend, or saying "look at that" to the person beside you.
savoring means forcing yourself to be cheerful
it's staying with good moments already there. it isn't forced cheer, and it isn't a fix for grief.

games.q: the Preacher of Ecclesiastes knows everything passes. what does he say to do with bread and wine?
o: eat and drink with joy and a merry heart.
save them for a better day.
games.why: "go thy way, eat thy bread with joy." because things pass, he says take them fully while they're here.

practice: Look back over the last day or two for something good, even small: a laugh, a meal, a message, a patch of sun. Go back into it slowly, where you were, what you heard, what the light was like, and let it play.
If nothing comes easily, savor this breath instead: the air in, the air out, the chair holding you.

wordCard.voice: The science of savoring. Noticing a good moment and staying with it, forward, now or looking back, so it lasts longer. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: savor. Good moments arrive all the time, and some of them can stay. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bryant, F. B., and Veroff, J., Savoring: A New Model of Positive Experience (2007)
